utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. The matter for today is a Status Conference. I see all accused and counsel are present. Perhaps the registrar would call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-66-PT, the Prosecutor versus Fatmir Limaj, Haradin Bala, and Isak Musliu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours. My name is Cayley. I appear on behalf of the Prosecutor with my colleagues, to my right Mr. Colin Black and to his right Mr. Hasan Younis. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Cayley. For the accused Mr. Limaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Michael Mansfield and I'm leading with Karim Khan for Fatmir Limaj. And may I say, as it's my first appearance here, and in -- especially in front of Your Honour, I'm greatly honoured to be here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We look forward to your company and those of other counsel over the few months to come. For Mr. Bala.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. My name is Gregor Guy-Smith and I have the honour of representing Mr. Bala, with my counsel, co-counsel, Mr. Richard Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. And for the third accused. Mr. Musliu.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Michael Topolski and I lead with Steven Powles on behalf of Isak Musliu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Who just comes into view around the pole that I've ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: He frequently hides away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will attempt to draw him out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I will do my very best, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Topolski. You will be aware that this trial Chamber, comprising Judge Thelin and Judge Van Den Wyngaert and myself have been assigned to the trial of this matter by order of the President, made on the 11th of October this year. Could I ask of each of the accused, firstly, Mr. Limaj, whether you are able to follow the proceedings from the interpretation that is being given to you. THE ACCUSED LIMAJ: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And of Mr. Bala.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. THE ACCUSED BALA: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And Mr. Musliu.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you repeat that just a little louder, please. THE ACCUSED MUSLIU: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand. I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The purpose of this Status Conference, so that the accused directly understand, is to seek to organise and ensure the smooth exchange between the parties of materials necessary for the expeditious preparation of the trial, and also to allow issues to be raised by counsel that may affect the running of the trial, and also to allow to any accused who has reason, an opportunity to raise issues in relation to their mental and physically condition, if that should be of any relevance. The Chamber itself has no particular issue which it wants to bring to the notice of the parties in this matter, so I would ask first whether, on the part of the Prosecution, there is any matter that it seemed appropriate to bring to the attention of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, there's only actually one issue that I have immediately, and that is compliance with Rule 68. And it would only be if Your Honour actually wanted me to give a brief summary of the steps that we have taken to comply with that particular Rule of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I say that it may be more expeditious to wait to see if it there is any perceived difficulty with what has occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll move on, then. Mr. Mansfield, is there any matter that your client wishes to bring forward?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. I will go slowly in case there are interpretation or translation difficulties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You'll find that's a habit which much grow upon you here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: May I say I'm engaged in a trial in London where it's all translated at the moment, so I'm rather used to a situation of speaking slowly. But if it's too slow then please say. However, there are particularly three interrelated matters that I wish to raise on behalf of Fatmir Limaj, although there -- I think some of them affect others as well. And they go to the heart, we say, of what this Tribunal is established to accomplish, which is a fair trial, and Article 6 compliance in terms of the convention itself. And the way we would ask you to consider that there is a risk, and I put it no higher at the moment, a risk of that convention right being in jeopardy arises in three ways. One is a decision which I appreciate isn't yours and is not one that Your Honours will be deciding in the next few days, and that concerns one that was made on the 14th of October, concerning all three defendants being kept, can I put it in shorthand form, incommunicado, save for communications with their lawyers and also diplomatic or consular staff. The second matter, and also related, is the condition in which they are transported to this court, which has recurred today, only worse. Third is the recurrent suggestion and innuendo that in some way or another, and of course it relates to the first two, no doubt, or certainly the first one, that there has been some kind in this case of witness intimidation, never spelt out, never detailed. May I deal with these three, because the three have to be seen together for their cumulative effect. It is singular in this case, particularly in relation to the first two issues, that these particular defendants and not any others appearing in this building that we're aware of, are being ordered to be held incommunicado and are being brought here with blindfolds as well as handcuffs, which are no doubt more customary. Why, in fact, these defendants should be singled out in this way is incomprehensible. But the effect, as you may imagine, is serious. It's serious in the sense that it creates a prejudicial atmosphere and a perception that decisions are already being made against their interest on assumptions that in some way or another they may be culpable. But in addition to that, of course, it affects their mental and physical welfare. And perhaps the last decision most of all, where they are being cut off altogether from the support of their families and friends. Now, that will have, particularly as it happens in the run-up to this trial, very deleterious effect on their ability to concentrate, their ability to focus, their ability to give instructions, and particularly at this time, when some of the most important witnesses that you are to hear from or may hear from, their identities have been revealed and preparation in relation to those witnesses has to be undertaken. So it is in the context of proximity to trial that the pressures that have been there from the beginning have now been exacerbated to such an extent that we are all concerned that the pressures in the end will result in none of them being in a fit position to countenance a trial. Now, one -- the first one, incommunicado, is a situation that I appreciate is being considered by the learned President at this moment, and a decision is expected early next week, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is this in respect of the decision of the Deputy Registrar?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Of the 14th of October?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: It is. It's a decision --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I've seen today a copy of that decision, and I have it before me now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And it should be dated, I think, the 14th of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And we have -- and I don't intend, obviously, to rehearse the representations that have been made to the President, because it's plainly a matter for him in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's a matter of the provision is made for appeal to the President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- from a decision such as this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. And we've availed ourselves of that provision. But the matter that I wish to put on record today, which relates not only to that issue that is, if I may say so, being considered separately, but also to the second issue, the question of blindfolds. And that is this: That the commander of the unit here in The Hague, Mr. McFadden, has been directly spoken to, certainly by counsel, but also by the defendant I represent. And I want it made clear, at least so far as he is concerned, that there is no suggestion from the Detention Unit itself that there has been at any stage a violation of any of the detention rules or the regime that governs their custody. In other words, no violation in terms of communicating with others in a way that they shouldn't, either over the telephone or by letter or in person. And it is, we say, somewhat remarkable that there doesn't appear to have been obtained, either for the purposes of blindfolding or, of course, for the matter of incommunicado, so far as we're aware, any report from the Detention Unit supporting any of the suggestions that are now being made. And we would ask so far as this second matter, that is the matter of blindfolds as concerned, that the matter is now long overdue for resolution. Because this issue, the question of being brought here in blindfolds, was raised earlier this year before the Pre-Trial Judge who was sitting at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to keep interrupting you, as I am, Mr. Mansfield, but I'm just wanting to get clear what it is. It's in respect of transport to and from the Detention Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Not in the Detention Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Not in the Detention Centre. To and from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And just so that it's clear, we've checked today. I wouldn't have raised it today if in fact the whole thing had changed, but it hasn't. It's very tight handcuffs today and also blindfolds. As far as I understand for the whole journey today. There was a time when the blindfolds were for the first bit of the journey and the last bit but not the bit in between. However, what we say about this is that -- and we have been saying it for some time, the dates on which this matter has arisen before was the 25th of February this year, the 26th of February this year, and the 27th of February, and then that's three occasions, and then the fourth occasion we've asked that you have a transcript, because it's -- of its significance. On Friday, the 25th of June, it was raised again at that stage in front of His Honour Judge Martin Canivell. And may I just direct your attention if you have either hard copies or you have it on screen, I think you have hard copies of this. May I just pause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Not I. No, we do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: We have some spares. I don't intend to obviously go through the whole of the transcript, just a part of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Any particular page?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. If Your Honour has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There's no reason to copy if that's what's being contemplated at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Could I start with a passage at the bottom of page -- I'm using the pagination top right-hand corner. Page 139, where Mr. Topolski at this stage is addressing the Tribunal about the situation and in particular going through the various Rules that apply. And at the bottom of the page, he's reached, page 919 of the current edition of the International Archbold Rule 90, an important rule: "Detainees shall at all times be transported in vehicles with adequate ventilation and light and in such a way and will not subject them to unnecessary physical hardship or indignity." Now, we say, of course, that is particularly pertinent. On the next page, 140, halfway down, Mr. Topolski at that stage had asked that a senior officer be available to answer questions, because there wasn't one there then or on that day he was addressing them. Now, so far as we know, if I may just elaborate that, as far as we know, there isn't any material being provided to indicate that this is necessary or why it is necessary. And if what we have been told by Mr. McFadden is correct, there is no need for these blindfolds. There may not be any need for handcuffs either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You've mentioned the head of the Detention Centre twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The issue is, I think, one that should be put differently. It is not subject to his control, nor subject to the Registry of this Tribunal, that the transportation of your clients occurs. There is an agreement between the United Nations and the host country.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And the responsibility for transportation under that agreement is entirely that of the host country, that is, the Kingdom of the Netherlands. And so it is their officers and their security decisions which determine how transportation occurs. And I think that's why I was interested earlier when you were mentioning the Detention Unit, whether it occurred in the Detention Unit or merely in the transfer of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: It occurs in the transfer. We do appreciate the responsibilities are divided, but the point we wish to make here is that there doesn't seem from any quarter, whosever the responsibility is, there's no evidence emanating from whatever quarter whoever took the decision for blindfolds had a reasonable basis for that decision. And we've been seeking from some quarter or another what the basis is. Now, if I -- I may just develop what was said on the last occasion. In fact, on the next page, His Honour is not very happy - it's page 141 - with the situation. And he'd had apparently on a previous occasion expressed his thoughts about it. And he goes on at line 11, he regrets it very much, because the situation he obviously is predicting may occur, at line 16, is that it could be repeated almost every day during the actual hearing. And he is saying that he will call again the attention of the Registrar to this point. And at the bottom of the page, if it doesn't go to a good solution in the near future - this is again in June - and I keep still being the Pre-Trial Judge in this case, to try to, well, push a little bit the matter so as not a little bit, as far as would be necessary with the Ministry of Justice, to find a suitable solution, which I'm very well aware of the matter. And then over the page again at 141, he wants to hear from Mr. Cayley. Mr. Cayley's response is interesting, because he is not indicating there that there's any direct or indirect evidence that whatever may be the thoughts of certain witnesses and so on, that in fact it has emanated from these defendants. And in fact, we reiterate. We've never been provided with any evidence, indirect or direct, that should suggest the need for blindfolds, or the incommunicado, which is the separate issue. It's a very vague response. And then it devolves into protocols, which I'll come back to. And then at the end of this matter, well, towards the end, there is the -- His Honour is indicating that what he's intending to do is to look into the matter and ask for an early resolution, is the way that it's being put. That's at the top of 148. Try and devise a solution, a prompt solution, for all of this. Now, I've only picked out some passages that are relevant to the question of why this process, demeaning and intimidating process, is continuing. What is remarkable, if I may say so, is that after June there hasn't been a single word said about this. We haven't had any communication from anybody indicating what discussions have taken place, if any, and on what occasion, and what resolution has been reached. It may be there isn't any. But judging by what's happened today, the matter is worse than it was in June and on the earlier occasions. And we would submit that if, again, bearing in mind the fair trial provisions, that with the trial not so very long away, this matter should have been resolved by now in such a way that, for example, if it's necessary that they don't see the trees outside on the way here because there's some suggestion they might organise something from inside the van, well, do what they do in England and I dare say in Australia and other jurisdictions. You have highly secure vehicles from which people can't -- they have light and air but they can't actually see out as a matter of course but they're not brought shackled with blindfolds. So we make a very simple point. This must be capable of early and, we say, easy resolution as no doubt was in the mind of His Honour in June. So we would ask if Your Honours would be kind enough today, to accelerate this process so that next week, along with the decision which will be determined in relation to the first issue, incommunicado, this could be at least decided so that these defendants know that in future, their transportation is going to be, if I may put it, at least humane. Now, may I just turn from that for a moment to the third matter I mentioned, and that's the question of the alleged intimidation of witnesses, with which allegation we are very concerned to rebut. Once again there has in fact in all the correspondence been little or no indication of the basis for this. We suspect it's coming from people who may generally be afraid, as often happens in criminal trials, domestic and international, may have nothing to do with these particular defendants or it may be that it's concerned with the perception that they have of things that have happened in the past. And we wish to emphasise, and I say this on behalf of certainly those who represent Fatmir Limaj, we were very conscious, certainly when I took over the lead role in this particular case, of recognising that the risks, recognising that we were dealing with what had been a theatre of war at one stage, and that therefore there were, if I may put it, sensitivities, raw sensitivities, that had to be dealt with extremely carefully. And last October - I've asked if they can be produced, but at the moment, I don't think they've been found - we sat down in Kosovo with a team of people and we drew up, on behalf of Mr. Limaj, and I drafted them myself, a set of protocols. They were very detailed, both for the management of an office there concerned with correlating all the information coming from here as well as information in Kosovo, and also protocols for an investigative team. They were carefully drafted and they were based on my junior and my own experience in England throughout 30 to 40 years of being familiar with how crime is investigated in England. One appreciates there are obviously going to be differences. But we were extremely conscious of the need to ensure that in fact there could be no suggestion that witnesses were being cajoled, they were being, as it were, dragged in to make statements or whatever. And as far as I'm aware, the protocols that we drew up last October, which were filed with this court, so that you were -- I don't mean you personally, but the court, the Tribunal were made aware at a very early stage that we had intended that everything should be entirely aboveboard and known by the Tribunal, not only as to the structure, but also the process itself. And we are very concerned that there are continuing suggestions in correspondence that something, never specified, has gone wrong at some stage or another. And so we would ask that care is taken when suggestions like this are made, because it contributes to the climate that I suggested that is being created, a climate of prejudice and hostility towards these defendants. I don't suggest, of course, that it relates to Your Honour or those who sit with you, but I do suggest that one -- care has to be taken by those who prosecute this case, if those are going to continue in that way. Now, there is one final matter, if I may raise it quickly, because I know others wish to address you, possibly on the same matters, but others as well. But this one again concerns all of us. It was only on the 20th are October, two days ago, that the statements unredacted were finally served and I think some of my friends haven't received them yet or have received them elsewhere. We would therefore ask if Your Honour would kindly consider the 30-day rule with regard to that matter such that the trial begins one week later, in November, namely, the 22nd, which would allow for the 30-day gap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: When did you receive the material?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I'm fairly sure mine arrived, I think on the 20th.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters ask that Mr. Mansfield slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And Mr. Topolski's was the same. I can't speak for others. But that was the date on which they arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So you effectively would seek a one-week delay in the trial commencement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much for that, Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Anything that --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, would it be possible, as you wish, for me to respond in turn to the matters raised by each Defence counsel or would you rather I respond at the end to all matters raised?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I say, Mr. Cayley, I was about to ask of the other two leading Defence counsel whether they joined in the submissions that have been put by Mr. Mansfield, because from what I would understand, all four points that he makes would appear to be common to the other accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour, and we would be joining in those remarks made by Mr. Mansfield on all points. And for purposes of the Court's understanding, with regard to the issue of when we received the latest disclosures, that also was on the 20th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I see. Thank you. And is that the position, Mr. Topolski, as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is. May I, I hope, to help, not repeat, what has already been submitted, add one or two matters of our own, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And can I deal with them I think in the same order that Mr. Mansfield did. First of all, under the heading of incommunicado and that decision, we are anxious to make it clear from here on in that our client and I imagine the two who sit either side of him, have hitherto held this Tribunal and all it stands for and its processes respectfully. They have put their faith and trust in this Tribunal to come to a just decision in their cases. The decision regarding incommunicado and the manner of it being sought and the manner of it being obtained has done nothing but sap my client's confidence in this Tribunal to do justice, such that he is telling me today, for the first time, that his capacity to prepare for his own defence has been seriously and significantly undermined by him not being able to do what every other human being is able to do in the world who is not incarcerated or dead, communicate with those he loves. To such an extent, again for the first time, he is asking me to arrange for him to be seen medically. He is very concerned as to his own psychological state. I raise the matter only because they are matters of concern. I raise it deferentially, respectfully, but I hope, hopefully, to indicate how important this is as far as he is concerned. I repeat: For him our understanding that there has been no infringement or violation of any rule or sub-rule or sub-sub-rule within the Detention Centre through the entirety of his own detention. May I, Your Honour, please pick up a point you made in discussion with Mr. Mansfield, and again, deferentially but respectfully differ as to the demarkation of responsibility here as between this Tribunal, the Ministry of Justice, and those responsible therefor by respectfully reminding the Court, and reminding is the word I used advisedly of course of the rules governing detention. I raised them with Judge Canivell and I repeat them now for the record if I may. I don't know if Your Honours have conveniently to hand Archbold International Criminal Court's practice, but it's to be found at page 906. I quoted it to Judge Canivell and it is to be found at page 138 of the official -- of the transcript of the hearing in June. And the point is this, and the rule says this: That the United Nations shall retain the ultimate responsibility and liability for all aspects of detention pursuant to these rules. All detainees shall be subject to the sole jurisdiction of the Tribunal at all times that they are so detained, even though physically absent from the Detention Unit, until final release or transfer to another institution. I forensically underline, as it were, the words "sole jurisdiction" of the Tribunal. If this is a matter for the Dutch authorities and not ultimately a matter for this Tribunal, which we respectfully submit it is, by its own rules, then that would involve us potentially in litigating the matter in the local courts. That cannot be in anyone's interest, nor is it appropriate and nor, we would respectfully submit, is it necessary. This court, as we submitted to Canivell, has the jurisdiction to rule upon the issue of the manner in which these men are brought uniquely to this building. The only other matter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Not uniquely, I gather.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Then Your Honour has more information than we ever have been given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I know only of history, not of present affairs. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I take the point. Nonetheless, the point remains undiminished, may I respectfully submit, notwithstanding that. Your Honour, may I say this only about witness intimidation. I've been described as being the driving force behind the protocol that exists in writing, and I think the Court should have a copy of it in front of you if you don't already, of the protocol that was drawn up between the Defence teams and the Office of the Prosecutor regarding the management of witnessing -- witnesses and their interviewing. As the driving force behind it, if that's the right term, it is nothing short of disturbing, not to say disappointing, that the correspondence that continues to emanate from the Office of the Prosecutor casts aspersions not only on my team but inferentially therefore on my team as its leader. This does nothing but generate more heat than light. It does nothing but accentuate the undermining of the Tribunal and its work in the eyes of the person I represent. As far as the question of the trial date is concerned, I have nothing to add to that application that Mr. Mansfield has already made. They are the submissions we make at this stage. I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Topolski. Now, Mr. Cayley, I might turn to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'll deal with the issues in the same order as Mr. Mansfield. I have a great deal less to say on them than he does, because a number of them do not concern the Office of the Prosecutor. In respect of the ban on communications, I can state to this Court that that ban was made upon the basis of evidence that was placed before the Registrar by this office. I believe it was done in a responsible fashion. I believe it was done in order to protect witnesses on the ground. That matter is now before the President of this Tribunal, and he is the one who will resolve that issue, not this Court. In respect of the second issue -- actually, one further point I would add. Mr. Mansfield states that these were the only accused who were being held incommunicado. That is not true. That is not true. That measure has been used in respect of other accused who have abused the communications privileges that they have at the UN Detention Unit. On the second issue of the manner in which the three accused are brought from the Detention Centre to this court, this is not a matter which the Prosecutor has any affect over whatsoever, so I will make no comment on it other than, in a sense, I do agree with the Defence that it should be resolved, because it was raised in June, and many months have passed. On the final issue, Your Honours, of witness intimidation, I would like to go into private session, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you give a brief subtle indication of the reasons?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wish to speak about matters which I do not wish to be transmitted to the public. I think some of the issues I raise may actually exacerbate problems in the region, frankly. And I would like to address you in private session, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, in terms of the last issue that was raised and the late disclosure of witness statements, if I can explain exactly the background to this. These were a number of witnesses who are protected witnesses. In order to ensure compliance with the disclosure regime, we disclosed summaries of their evidence to the Defence. So it's not as if the Defence have no idea what this evidence is about. All we did in those summaries was to take out identifying information about those witnesses. They were very scared. They didn't want their names disclosed until 30 days prior to the start of the trial. And that -- the original Trial Chamber agreed with. Now, rather than delaying the start of this trial, my suggestion would be that we essentially drop any of those witnesses who fall within that group back into the -- or actually along into the trial process, which would essentially remedy any prejudice, and frankly, I don't think there is any prejudice to the Defence, because they've had the essence, they've had the fundamentals of this evidence now for well over a year. And so I don't think there is any prejudice. But if there is a perceived prejudice, we can ensure that none of those witnesses appear in the first seven days of the trial, thus complying with the 30-day disclosure period with which the Defence are concerned. And that way, we don't need to delay the start of the trial. And again, I apologise. Unfortunately, the manner in which statements are transported is not always predictable. We use these parcels from UPS, and I think probably I was a bit late myself in ensuring that it went out. So I apologise to the Court and I apologise to Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cayley. I don't think there's any matter that really calls for direct responsive submission unless something burns in the heart of any counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: It's not that I'm sitting on a hot seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I didn't identify which part of the body, Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: There is one matter, if I may respond to it, which has been raised. As far as I know, it's the first time it's been raised. I've just had a quick consultation. It may apply to others as well. What we are particularly concerned about is the suggestion today that the Prosecution are going to lead before the Tribunal evidence of a systematic and organised campaign of some form, presumably, of intimidation or inference or something. Now, if this is going to become an element of trial, as I anticipated it would, in the way that correspondence has been certainly held in over the past year, then we are concerned, certainly in terms of the trial date start, certainly in terms of when are we going to receive this material, and how is it relevant. Because you will have noticed in what has been said, it's extraordinarily vague, it is not suggested that it has anything to do with those who represent these defendants. In fact, it's not actually suggested it's any of these defendants. Who are the people who purport to represent them? What is being said here? Now, I'm not asking for identities, but the suggestion here is again innuendo, it's indirect, and of course, my learned friend may say he's never come across it before. May I say on behalf of these defendants: We've never come across a situation like this before where the Prosecution intend to make part of their case suggested interference along with all the other matters I've raised, namely, incommunicado and blindfolds. Your Honour, we've been involved and certainly I've been involved in over the last 30 or 40 years in cases of equal gravity to this where suggestions have been made, and there's one at the moment in London, of considerable gravity in terms of undermining the fabric of society, intending to cause enormous damage to a large number of people. It's much larger than this case, in fact, and they are serious crimes that have been alleged. At no stage in any of those prosecutions have defendants been blindfolded, have they been made incommunicado, still less as the Prosecution said they're going to introduce allegations of intimidation into the trial itself. So we say this trial is spiralling into an arena in which it should not go, unless it is going to be said that it's relevant to a particular evidence that is relevant, as opposed to peripheral, and it can be shown with clear material that we can deal with in advance, unless it's all going to be done as it were behind closed doors. So we are disturbed by what is now being said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I take it, gentlemen, that your content for the matter to rest at that. Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I've become increasingly concerned about what I would term as the chilling effect that is occurring with regard to my client's ability to adequately and properly be defended and defend himself in regard to some of the statements just made. I'm also somewhat concerned because the remarks made by my colleague, Mr. Cayley here, were quite conclusory in nature and I feel we're in a fashion having to respond to allegations for which there are no identities, which puts us in a position of fighting phantoms and ghosts, and the phantoms and ghosts that we are fighting are extremely prejudicial to the fair consideration of the matters that are before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Topolski, anything to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: May I again I hope helpfully only add this: What Mr. Cayley has said to Your Honours this afternoon has an echo. In fact, it has an echo in print. It's a letter of the 15th of October to he wrote to all of us defending these defendants, from which I quote one line: "The Prosecution has in fact learned that in five instances individuals representing the Defence have approached" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for interpretation and the record --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: -- "or encouraged them to come to an interview with the Defence. That is described as a blatant violation of the protocol."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speaker is not being interpreted at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The request is that you go a little slower, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. Old habits die very hard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The process of interpretation is to move from one language to another to another and that takes longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I'm terribly sorry. I hope that's the last time you have to stop me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I am advised that it may help if you find it a problem to have your earpieces on and you can then get an idea of how the interpretation is progressing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Can I just say, then, for the benefit of those who are interpreting, that what I have been submitting is that what Mr. Cayley has been saying to us this afternoon when in closed session has an echo in a letter, simply making an allegation of five instances, I quote: "Individuals representing the Defence have approached Prosecution witnesses." For my part, I have no hesitation in asking now the identity of those people. Is it being said they're members of my team, Mr. Limaj, Mr. Bala, or none, or all three, or some of each? I hope the point is clear. If there are such people conducting themselves in this way, I should like to know about it so I can take instructions and I can deal with it. That, I hope, expresses, in the clearest possible, simple, not to say simplistic terms, how seriously we take this, and I echo, endorse, and underline Mr. Mansfield's suggestion. I may not have been about for 40 years, only a little less than that, and in my experience it's slightly unusual not to say unique for the Crown to be seeking to lead evidence of this kind, in proof of this indictment, but that's perhaps a matter for another day. They are the submissions we make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The matter which is of concern because of its capacity to inflame, at a time when calm is important, is the third of the four matters raised by Mr. Mansfield and the counsel for each of the other accused, that is, the matter of approach as to witnesses. The Chamber is in no way privy to what has passed between counsel in this matter, and at the moment, the position from the point of view of the Chamber is that there has been a foreshadowing of the possibility of evidence being led in the trial concerning inference with witnesses. If and when that should become in some way a reality, in other words, specific notice is given or evidence is sought to be led on matter, the Chamber will naturally then deal with the matter on its merit. It would be erroneous and not helpful for us to attempt, in theory, to deal with this issue at the present time. So it is a matter for the future, not for today. I would suggest that if there remains indecision or uncertainty as to whether it is suggested that the Defence teams, if I can use that more general word, of any one or more of the accused is in some way involved in improper conduct, that that matter should be raised between counsel, with a view to having the position clarified. And we are grateful in particular, Mr. Topolski, for your indication, which is position and attitude we would expect of counsel if there were any suggestion of impropriety. If we could turn to other matters. The first order that has been made by the Deputy Registrar and which, as I've indicated, we saw today is under the Rules a matter now within the jurisdiction of the President and it will be clearly dealt with by him in due course. Therefore, it would not be appropriate for this Trial Chamber to comment upon it, and it is not open to us to take any step in respect of it at the present time. But the procedures are there. They are there not only for the protection of the processes of the Tribunal but also to ensure the fairness of proceedings before the Tribunal, and those matters will be dealt with by the appropriate authority, in this case, the President. The second matter raised, that of the blindfolding during the transportation, is a matter over which there is some confusion and uncertainty. At least, that is the indication we have from the various submissions that have been put to us. Our understanding of the matter is that the sole responsibility for security during the transport of prisoners outside of detention facilities and the premises of this Tribunal are those of the host country. Therefore, at this stage, we would urge counsel for each accused to approach first the Registrar, and then, with guidance from the Registrar as to the most appropriate people, to approach what I believe is the Ministry of Justice for the Netherlands, to raise the concerns there are about this matter. I could indicate that we will informally advise the Registrar that the matter has been raised and advise the Registrar that concerns that have been put to us by counsel on their face appear to have some substance, and that they have already seen what appears in the transcript before the Pre-Trial Judge about the matter. But beyond that, it is a matter for resolution with the Dutch authorities. If things go wrong in the transportation, the responsibility is theirs, the responsibility, therefore, for the measures taken is theirs. It would be well within the capacity of those representing the accused to put to the appropriate Dutch authorities suggestions for alternative means that might be adopted, as they've been briefly foreshadowed here, to avoid the matters that are giving concern to your clients but which, at the same time, might well enable any concerns that those authorities have to be satisfactorily met. The fourth matter raised concerns the statements. It appears they have been served late. In the circumstances, given that the substance of them was earlier known and the undertaking of the Prosecution that they would not call any of the witnesses affected by the late delivery of the full statements until outside the 30-day rule, the Chamber would take the view that there is no reason to delay the commencement of the trial and that any embarrassment or difficulty caused by the lateness of the statements will be satisfactorily met by that delay in the order in which those witnesses are called. Is there any matter concerning the health of the accused or their conditions of actual detention that needs to be raised at the present time? Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: None, Your Honour. Not at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Only just to repeat that which I've already submitted, that we shall arrange for a psychiatric examination. There is grave concern on the part of my lay client as to that facility and its availability and suitability within the Detention Centre, but we shall take steps to assist in any way we can. May I, Your Honour, please, for the purposes of clarification only, simply ensure that I understand the decisions or indications that you've just made. It follows from them, it seems to me, that Judge Canivell was unable to make any progress in the discussions he indicated he might be having or somebody might be having with the Ministry of Justice on the question of blindfolds, and therefore we're not treading over ground. When we start to tread the ground that you've suggested we tread, it's already been trodden before to be met with "But we've already discussed this with Judge Canivell." May we take it discussions were not productive in any sense, in any sense of that word? Is that a fair way of proceeding?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would doubt that His Honour had any direct discussions with the ministry. I think his views may have been put to the Registry. It was for that reason that I suggested that counsel might first approach this Registry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And armed with the information that might there be available to you, your future course can be plotted out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I'm grateful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there any other matter that any counsel wishes to raise? If not, that concludes the matters that need to be dealt with at this Status Conference. We thank you all for your attendance, and we will obviously have occasion to see much of you in the near future. We will now adjourn.
